problem: Standard robot navigation ignores the semantic structure of human environments (rooms, doors, tables, signs) and treats people as obstacles, so robots cannot take human-friendly goals or behave appropriately around people, for example when following one through a door.
motivation: Human environments are designed for people, and service robots will work close to them. Semantic maps with user-provided labels allow named goals and let the robot infer user intent. Reactive person following causes deadlocks and social problems at doors and during labeling tasks.
key_idea: Build a SLAM map of planar and door-sign landmarks, let users label landmarks by having the robot follow them and by pointing gestures plus a phone app, then use the labeled semantic map to drive human-aware path planning and a 4-phase context-aware person-following state machine.
insight: Modeling pointing-gesture error statistics with a Mahalanobis distance disambiguates targets reliably, and correction helped Head-Hand at all separations; targets were unambiguous at 3 cm or more separation. Semantic context (near a landmark or door) lets the robot pick a better position than reactive following, which resolves the labeling-visibility and door-deadlock cases. All of this is shown qualitatively with proof-of-concept demos, not user studies.
method: Plane and door-sign SLAM: GTSAM factor graph with plane landmarks (normal, d, convex hull), JCBB data association, and door signs detected by HOG+SVM and read by GoogleGoggles OCR.
Person following: leg and torso laser detectors feed a constant-velocity Kalman filter; a DWA-style time-augmented tree with depth-limited BFS maximizes a goal function (about 1 m behind the human).

Pointing-gesture target estimation: elbow-hand and head-hand rays in spherical angles, bias correction from prior error statistics, Mahalanobis distance with a threshold and a ratio test to detect ambiguity.

Interactive labeling: the user selects 'Label Object' or 'Label Planar Surface' in the app and points; the target is the intersecting plane or the nearest cluster on a table (SURF model), and it receives the label.
Goal extraction: a single labeled plane gives a goal 1 m from its nearest hull vertex; multiple planes with the same label are treated as a region and the goal is the hull centroid.
Human-aware planning: A* static plan with path length, Gaussian safety and group disturbance costs, refined by a Social Forces Model dynamic planner, with DWA as the local planner.

Context-aware following: a Signal/Approach/Execution/Release state machine; for labeling, the robot samples poses in the user-landmark p-space with Score=1-Cost_vis-Cost_obs; for doors, it goes to the far side of the door after the user points.

setting.backbone: Classical pipeline: GTSAM SLAM, HOG+SVM door-sign detector, GoogleGoggles OCR, Kalman filter, DWA/A*/Social Forces, OpenNI NITE skeleton tracker
setting.training_data: Small: SVM sign classifier, leg classifier, and pointing error statistics from 6 users x 7 targets x 30 frames
setting.observation: Laser scanners (ankle and torso height), RGB-D (Xtion/Kinect), head laser, phone app input
setting.action_space: continuous velocity commands (v, omega) via DWA on a Segway base
setting.simulator: real world (plus a simple planning simulation example)
setting.privileged: none (a semantic map is built interactively; user is assumed cooperative, objects assumed unique and static)

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is evaluated. Only person-following statistics (7 subjects, about 1.2 km, average distance 1.16 m) and pointing-error statistics are reported, and these are not benchmark numbers.
results: The person follower followed 7 subjects for about 1.2 km with no collisions and an average distance of 1.16 m. In the pointing separation test, the intended object always had a corrected D_mah below 2, and targets were ambiguous only at 2 cm separation. Context-aware labeling and door-passing behaviors and human-aware path planning were demonstrated qualitatively, with no baseline comparison.
limitations: Evaluation is qualitative and small-scale, with demos by a knowledgeable user, no user study with novices, and no baseline comparison.
Assumes static, unique objects and relies on door signs and correct pointing direction; multiple nearby doors and door orientation are not handled.
Only implicit robot-human communication through motion, with no dialogue or gaze.
